author: Maharnav Bhuyan
title: Labor and One Nation compete to arrest their way out of a mental health crisis
content:
Labor and One Nation agree on almost nothing, with the exception being on crime, where they read from the same script.

Premier Ben Carroll wants 1500 more police. One Nation wants more police, harsher treatment of repeat offenders and a 24/7 bail court. Its campaign launch promised to make Victoria the toughest state on crime. The Coalition has simply raised the bid to 3000. Labor's Attorney-General insists “tough bail is working”.

Victoria has run this experiment before. Labor funded 3135 more police between 2016 and 2021. Over 2024-25, the number of criminal incidents hit its highest level since records began.

Ask Victoria Police what drives crime and the answer reads like a social policy brief.

In June, it named the cost of living, recidivism, organised crime and drugs. In September, it listed organised crime, recidivism, mental health and illicit drugs.

Who ends up on the inside? In the latest national survey of people entering prison, from last year, 51% had been diagnosed with a mental health condition and 73% had used illicit drugs in the past year. In the month before prison, 43% were homeless and 46% were unemployed.

These statistics show that rather than being hardened criminals, prisoners are people who have been failed by a squeezed economy, a broken health system and by communities with nowhere to turn.

When people do reach out, the door is often shut.

About 4550 Victorians were waiting for drug and alcohol treatment on any given day last year. In June 2025, 14 men sat in custody waiting for a bed at Thomas Embling, the state’s secure psychiatric hospital. Victoria’s own royal commission found the mental health system had “catastrophically failed”.

On November 6, HungryPanda rider Feng Jianming was stabbed to death near the Queen Victoria Market. He was 47, a father of two, and had spent nine years working here to support his family. A second rider was seriously injured.

Roberto Urbano, 51, has been charged with the murder. He is presumed innocent, but the court has already seen something every politician promising more police should think about. Urbano’s lawyer told the court that he experiences schizophrenia.

Appearing by video link from a police cell, in front of a magistrate, Urbano stood on a stool and exposed himself to the courtroom. Police custody, a camera and a magistrate; there is no more heavily-policed place. If the law cannot reach a person in that state, another 1500 police officers on the street certainly will not.

People in a mental health crisis need care; they need treatment before things fall apart. Was Urbano seeing a doctor? Did he have somewhere safe to live? Those are the questions this case should prompt every party running in the election to answer.

None of this means people with mental illness are dangerous; they are several times more likely than others to be assaulted.

The lesson is simple: A society where vulnerable people can ask for help and get it is a safer society.

Instead, the money flows to prison cells. Since Labor’s “toughest bail laws in Australia” began in March last year, the prison population has grown by about 19%.

This year’s state budget found $229 million for new prison beds and $43 million for programs that keep people out of them.

Each prisoner costs the public purse almost $600 a day and more than a third of those released are back inside within two years.

One Nation’s other big idea — tougher sentences — is weaker still.

The Coalition offers more of the same. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson’s 3000 extra police would include recruits from Britain, Ireland and New Zealand.

The Coalition also promises a “one-strike” bail rule for serious offences and has promised to expand Adult Time for Violent Crime from eight offences to 20. Youth diversion gets a mention after the police, bail and sentencing pledges.

The Victorian Sentencing Advisory Council found that longer prison terms do not produce a matching increase in deterrence. A longer stretch inside does not treat what it was that put the person there.

You cannot handcuff the cost of living. You cannot arrest a mental illness.

This is not a call on parties to be “soft” on crime. It is about being more serious about crime prevention. That means funding mental health and drug treatment until the queues disappear. It means building the forensic beds, called for by the royal commission. People leaving prison need secure homes to go to. Nationally, a third expect to be homeless on release.

There needs to be investment in the struggling suburbs and towns, where disadvantage and prison admissions pile up.

Before buying another 1500 uniforms, find out why people end up in a cell.

Victoria should fund an independent, ongoing study that asks thousands of people in its prisons what went wrong in their lives, and tie prevention budgets to the answers.

Communities have shown another way. In Bourke, in north-west NSW, the Aboriginal-led Maranguka project, guided by the Bourke Tribal Council, has spent more than a decade shifting the focus from punishment to community-led solutions.

Labor and One Nation are selling the same police band-aid, but in different colours. Until we ask why are people ending up in a cell, the public will keep paying for more cells and more cops, and there will be more grieving families.

Before November 28, ask your candidates one question: What will you do before the crime, not after it?

author: Cas Smith
title: Hazelmere locals reject plans for mega AI data centre
content:
About 200 people rallied outside Midland Town Hall on November 11 to oppose plans for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs.

Gwenaël (Gwen) Velge, a Research Associate at Murdoch University’s Mineral Policy Institute; Kate Herron from Trillion Trees; and former Labor MLA Matthew Hughes addressed the rally and highlighted the disruptive nature of CDC Data Centres’ planned project, which is expected to cause significant noise pollution and energy usage.

At a consultation meeting last month, a CDC technician said the data centre would have an energy allotment of 192 megawatts (MW) with 96 generators.

This would make it significantly larger than the 120 MW, 88 generator data centre previously proposed by Greensquare, which was rejected earlier this year by the City of Swan, following community backlash and concerns about noise pollution.

Velge noted the significance of this decision in the Mining Monitor on October 29. “Earlier this year, the City recommended refusing the GreenSquare proposal over the potential noise of its 88 generators.

“CDC proposes 96 generators, [which] come within 1dB (decibels) of the limit modelled at 75% load, and approach ‘the limits of compliance’; whereas Greensquare was asked to model at 100% load.”

He said the “sheer scale” of the energy demand of hyperscale data centres makes it harder to achieve a renewable energy transition.

“Renewable energy capacity meant to replace coal and gas is directly absorbed by this new demand. In the best-case scenario, this added demand slows down the transition, in the worst-case scenario the narrative and promises of ‘transition’ justifies and legitimates actual energy addition.

“Of course, some grid growth is to be expected as we electrify. But data centres are a clear case of addition: that demand did not exist before and it competes directly with the electrification part of the transition.”

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) expects consumption on the region’s electrical grid to increase by 57% in the next decade, from 20.4 to 32.1 terrawatt-hours (TWh).

However, this excludes the energy demands from data centre projects already in the pipeline, which are expected to be excessive, based on the ‘cooling’ requirement for servers.

Two planned projects in WA, the Hazelmere data centre and a project in Maddington — both proposed by CDC — are expected to consume 4.3TWh a year in total (or on a single hot day, up to 550–590MW).

Velge said this would be “more than five times AEMO’s forecast for the entire sector, and nearly 40% of the total projected growth for the next decade”.

“With huge amounts of heat comes huge amounts of emissions, and heat which must be displaced with either water or with fans.

“So, the choice is between huge water usage or noise. Adding this much extra demand on the grid is bound to push the price of electricity much higher than it already is.”

Another concern is the lack of transparency around the Hazelmere project, with many questions remaining about how it might develop. CDC’s application, for example, refers to the planned building as “HA1”, which raises the question: should people be expecting a HA2?

Local residents have discovered that CDC has acquired the adjoining lots at 170 Bushmead Road and 40 and 50 Hazelmere Crescent, making a larger project down the track a real possibility, even if the acquisitions had not been included in the current application.

This meant that CDC could be using a “salami-slicing” approach, splitting the project into smaller units, so that its cumulative impacts can’t be assessed as a whole.

In any case, Gwen argued that data centre projects should be approached like mining ones.

“Treating data centres like mining projects means applying our Mining Policy Principles: the right of affected communities to veto, assessment of cumulative impacts not just project by project assessments and a meaningful test of whether the project serves communities and the transition or if it serves private profits....

“We shouldn’t let ourselves be priced out of our own public utilities to release more carbon emissions and more heat into our globally warming atmosphere.

“As we know from the US, data centres are also an opportunity to rally people from all walks of life and all political stripes around something everyone opposes — a genuinely positive sight in the polarising times we live in.

“The numbers don’t add up. People and ecosystems will be left paying the price. We can still say no.”

author: Wendy Bacon, Cathy Peters
title: Time to reassess the antisemitism envoy’s role
content:
Civil liberties and Palestinian supporters are calling for the Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, to be sacked after her latest report accused them of using “human rights” to hide their antisemitism.

Segal’s Plan to Combat Antisemitism appears designed to raise the pressure on all levels of government as well as the forthcoming final report of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion in December.

Segal is an active player in an international network, coordinated by key pro-Israel Jewish bodies as well as the United States State Department. Indeed, if it had not been for pressure from the US government, Segal might not have the job at all.

Segal is one of 32 Special Envoys in North America, Europe, South America, Israel and Australia.

The position of the US Special Envoy to Combat and Monitor Antisemitism was established in 2004, when New Jersey Republican congressman Chris Smith, who has a history of advocating for Israel and a record of accusing organisations including UN bodies of rampant antisemitism, successfully pushed to pass legislation creating the position.

Following the US lead, the European Union appointed an Envoy in 2015, followed by Canada, Greece, the Organization of American States and Britain. Israel’s envoy is part of its Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In 2021, Smith, by then a strong supporter of Donald Trump, successfully pushed for an amendment which strengthened the position of US Special Envoy to the level of ambassador. They report directly to the Secretary of State, are appointed by the President and, crucially, can access foreign governments.

The ambassador’s mission is to promote US foreign policy by developing and implementing policies and projects to support action against antisemitism.

The office uses the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition, which directly links Jewish people with Zionism and the State of Israel, and conflates criticism of Israel with antisemitism.

The current US Antisemitism Ambassador is far right winger Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun. He has boasted about influencing governments and recently described his office as supporting Trump’s policies by having 250,000 visas cancelled to keep campuses “‘safe”, interfering in foreign educational curricula and initiating prosecutions of what he describes as “hate crimes”.

This is echoed in Segal’s plan, which include compulsory training for Home Affairs staff responsible for certain visa applications and a new task force to review existing visas.

While it was initially reluctant, the Anthony Albanese Labor government appointed Segal in July 2024, after intense lobbying from the US State Department, which the Australian media did not cover.

FOI releases show that in May 2024, Aaron Keyek, the then US deputy antisemitism envoy, met with Australian officials in Foreign Affairs and Trade and the Attorney General’s Department to pressure the Albanese government to appoint an envoy.

Keyek also met with Deborah O’Neill, the Co-Chair of Labor Friends of Israel.

The crunch came with an ultimatum regarding a meeting of special envoys in Argentina, in July 2024, to sign US-drafted global guidelines to counter antisemitism.

A former senior US official told Jerusalem News Syndicate: “We were all diplomatic about it, but we told Australia, essentially, ‘It’s going to be glaring’. We didn’t want to repeat the situation, where one of our closest allies didn’t stand up to one of the top foreign-policy priorities when it comes to human rights that the United States is pushing internationally… So we told them that they could only attend if the delegation was led by a special envoy.”

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade sent a cable to the US State Department on July 4 advising of the imminent appointment of an envoy who would report directly to the Prime Minister.

Segal was appointed on July 9, just 10 days before the meeting in Buenos Aires, which she attended. According to that cable, she had already approved the guidelines and her tickets had been booked before she was appointed.

Australia’s Ambassador to Argentina was permitted to sign off on the guidelines which refer to the IHRA definition as a key tool for fighting antisemitism, as a result of Segal’s hasty appointment.

In 2019 the New York based World Jewish Congress (WJC), the central governing organisation of Jewish organisations, which “defends the Jewish state of Israel”, established the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Network to coordinate “responses to antisemitism”.

Segal’s work is partially dictated by this body. Since her appointment, Segal has worked closely with SECCA. In July last year, Rabbi Yehuda, the US Special Envoy in the State Department Ambassador thanked her for hosting an online forum.

In her first 15 months, Segal took five overseas trips, costing $85,000, and in May she travelled to Geneva to sign another SECCA joint declaration.

The 15th meeting of SECCA was held last month in Dublin, organised by the WJC in partnership with the European Commission. The conference aimed to look at ways to implement strong measures to “confront online hatred and turn government promises into concrete action”.

It heard reports from delegates from 28 countries, including Australia, and included visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta. It included representatives from the WJC’s Technology and Human Rights institute, which focuses solely on lobbying governments, international bodies, and tech companies on policy, monitoring and control within the digital realm.

Maram Stern, WJC Executive Vice President and SECCA Co-Chair spoke at the forum emphasising the need to urgently enforce “practical solutions” to antisemitism.

Stern linked the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack to a worldwide surge in antisemitism, rather than to the worldwide revulsion with Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Segal. who spoke via video to the Dublin conference, urged stronger institutional accountability, education and enforcement against antisemitism.

Referring to the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion (which heard many unchallenged allegations of antisemitism), Segal noted that its proceedings had brought into focus “concerns about antisemitism in universities, cultural institutions, and healthcare”.

These are key areas where we have seen false claims of antisemitism and lawfare used against academics, artists and healthcare workers.

Segal was not the only Australian who spoke. Her close partners from the Executive Council of Australian Jewry (EJAC), Peter Wertheim, EJAC co-CEO, called for “more proactive regulation of technology companies and effective legal avenues for people harmed by online content”.

Daniel Aghion, ECAJ president and WJC vice president, emphasised the importance of active special envoys, sustained government engagement and coordination between Jewish organisations.

Before the conference had started, it emerged that one of Dublin’s prestigious hotels had refused to accommodate the SECCA delegates and alternative accommodation and a conference venue had to be found.

This went unreported until Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland, told a pre-conference event that the 4-star Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin, which had taken the SECCA booking for 70 rooms in April, had abruptly cancelled this booking after a meeting with the conference organisers and the hotel’s general manager.

Cohen was asked by the hotel manager whether the event had any ties to the Israeli Defence Force (IDF). He told Fox News Digital, “I was completely taken aback by that question. I said, ‘What would the IDF have to do with a conference on antisemitism?’.”

It was revealed that the hotel’s general manager subsequently consulted the hotel owners before the cancellation was made.

This was immediately characterised by the organisers as a major antisemitic event.

The World Jewish Congress published an opinion piece by Maurice Cohen on October 14 titled: “Ironically, an antisemitism conference falls victim to Jew-hatred”.

Although the Herbert Park Hotel refused to make public comment, it is clear it chose not to be associated with an event that had ties to the IDF.

The links between SECCA and support of Israel and members of the IDF are strong. SECCA representatives work with pro-Israel organisations, that have key personnel directly connected with the Israeli state, and past and present members of the IDF.

Conflating this refusal with antisemitism is yet another example of how peak pro-Israel Jewish organisations continue to wrongly link antisemitism to protest actions such as the Herbert Park Hotel boycott.

One of the major organisations participating in the SECCA conference in Dublin was the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM), which is based in the US and has spread internationally. Its advisory board members and its CEO are directly linked to Israel.

CAM works globally to pressure governments to not only endorse the IHRA definition of antisemitism but to enforce it. It reported that it was recognised as a “trusted US State Department partner” at the SECCA conference, where it reiterated the coordinated push to get governments to enforce the IHRA antisemitism definition — a point which was emphasised by US Special Envoy Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun.

CAM also has strong links with the IDF.

The J50 forum, founded by Israel’s foreign ministry, includes 50 Jewish organisations internationally. Its third meeting in Jerusalem last September issued its hard line and contentious Declaration on Zionism and Antisemitism, which stated unequivocally that “Zionism is part of Jewish identity”.

It defined anti-Zionism as a form of antisemitism when used to “marginalize or deny Jewish self-determination”.

Daniel Aghion’s presentation summarised ECAJ’s work since the Bondi terrorist attack. He offered some unguarded insights into how this organisation mobilised around the royal commission: “It has been a massive exercise over the last year. The Jewish community has spent millions of dollars, and many millions more in pro bono legal and non-legal work. This was to make sure that our voice is heard properly, both inside and outside the Commission, and to ensure that the Commission has run as well as it can.”

MWM asked ECAJ about whether any of ECAJ’s large government grants had been used on the royal commission work but not not receive a response.

On November 19, the Israel-based Jerusalem Post Group’s first Asia-Pacific Summit will be held in Sydney. It will feature many Israeli speakers, including Israel’s president Isaac Herzog’s wife Michel Herzog, who will speak online, the Israeli ambassador to Australia, former senior IDF members, as well as President of Zionist Federation of Australia, Jeremy Liebler.

The focus is on “countering hostility” to Israel and building business links, something which many anti-genocide Australians do not support.

Ten days later the 2026 CAM conference for mayors and councillors will be held in Sydney. These events reinforce the global messaging of SECCA, WJC and J50. They are designed to add impetus Segal’s agenda leading up to the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre, and prior to the release of the royal commission report in December.

Segal’s overreach into all aspects of our civil life is not just angering human rights activists, and those who are unfairly being labelled as antisemitic, but large sections of Australian society who do not support Israel and do not want to be policed at the service of this rogue state.

Albanese buckled to pressure in creating the position of antisemitism envoy and made a striking error in appointing the Israel lobby’s choice to that position.

As anger grows about Segal’s appointment, it is time to reassess the legitimacy of the position itself in light of the facts surrounding its creation.

We have existing anti-discrimination legislation and strong National Anti-Racism Framework guidelines that are yet to be implemented.

Bending to US, Israel and the local Israel lobby’s demands will only intensify public anger.

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Protesters condemn state government attacks on Palestine solidarity, free speech
content:
Rallies were held across the country on November 15 to express solidarity with the people of Palestine and oppose repression of speech and protest by all levels of government.

The national day of action against repressive laws was called by Justice for Palestine Magan-djin (JFP) as part of its campaign to repeal the Queensland Liberal National Party government’s laws which criminalise Palestine solidarity slogans including “From the river to the sea” and “Globalise the intifada [uprising]”.

Chris Minns’ NSW Labor government is supporting the Queensland LNP government in the High Court challenge brought by JFP to overturn the laws. Victorian Liberals leader Jess Wilson has vowed to ban the phrase “Globalise the intifada” if elected on November 28.

JFP spokesperson Remah Naji said repression is “uniting our political class” and “thousands of us are united in defending our right to protest genocide”.

“The crimes remain the crime of genocide, the crime of occupation and the crime of apartheid. There is no amount of repression that will distract us from Israel’s crimes or absolve our government from its complicity in them.”

Michael Bradley, from MARQUE Lawyers, which is representing JFP in the High Court Case, said: “Queensland is currently leading the way with its ridiculous law that criminalises mere words, but other states are watching and keen to follow suit.

“It is more critical than ever that a stand is taken — in the courts and on the street — to demand our basic rights: to assemble, to protest and to speak.”

The crack down comes as Israel continues to kill Palestinians in Gaza and the Occupied West Bank, despite the so-called ceasefire. Its strike on the Nasser Hospital on November 12 — the only functioning hospital in Gaza — which killed six people, including surgeon Dr Rizq Shaira and a teenage patient, was condemned by 18 countries for violating international law.

As winter floods, storms and cold descend, many are still left sheltering in tents because of Israel’s restriction of supplies into Gaza. A nine-month-old baby died from hypothermia in Khan Younis in Southern Gaza on November 12 due to exposure to extreme cold.

Israel has killed at least 1610 Palestinians since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

Jonathan Strauss reports that 500 people marched in Magan-djin/Brisbane behind a large banner featuring the banned slogan “From the river to the sea”, a frequent chant of the Palestine solidarity movement.

The other banned slogan, “Globalise the intifada”, was not commonly used at Palestine rallies in Magan-djin, but expresses a desire for international support for the Palestinian people.

Anti-Zionist Jewish activist Stephen Heydt told the crowd that “kifah” means “fight” in Arabic. At the end of his speech he and others revealed t-shirts with the “globalise” slogan.

Police soon forcefully intervened, arresting seven people throughout the rally, including Heydt and two women who had carried the lead banner.

Naji said genocide was the real crime, not protesting the complicty of the Queensland and federal government.

The seven arrests add to the 31 previously made under the anti-free speech laws. Some, like Heydt, have now been arrested twice.

JFP is pursuing a High Court challenge to strike down the anti-free speech laws. It is asking for financial support for this and is organising a fundraising event on December 11.

The rally also featured music from a local punk band and a Riff Raff brass contingent.

Pip Hinman reports from Gadigal Country/Sydney that hundreds took to the streets again for Gaza on November 15. They demanded that NSW and federal Labor take action for Palestine, and stop trying to suppress free speech — particularly those speaking up against genocide.

The protest was called to show solidarity with pro-Palestine supporters in Queensland, who are being criminalised for standing up against genocide, and called for the scrapping of bans on phrases which call for rights, dignity, peace and justice for those living between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.

Minns wants to bring in similar laws, but is waiting on the outcome of the High Court challenge.

Speakers at the protest included Dr Shamikh Badra, who is from Gaza. He called on the federal government to act for Palestine, and not allow the weapons trade to continue.

Badra condemned the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza. He said people were still being denied food, medical assistance and other aid, and recent floods had made their lives even more unbearable.

Sue Higginson, NSW Greens MLC, called on Labor to help. “The genocidal state of Israel will not let in the support. There are people [who have been] flooded, People have lost the only shelter they had — which was a flipping tent for goodness sake. And they can’t replace it.” She said Australia needs to impose a boycott, sanctions and divestment regime on Israel.

Meanwhile, foreign minister Penny Wong announced on November 16, that Australia had signed a joint statement with Canada, Italy and Britain urging Israel to allow “immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza ... before it is too late.”

Brian Mahony reports that protesters gathered in Gumbaynggirr Country/Coffs Harbour to join the November 15 national day of action to defend free speech and the right to protest.

Protesters also called for an end to Australia’s ongoing arms trade with Israel.

Cas Smith reports that about 300 people gathered at Russell Square in Boorloo/Perth on November 15 to call for an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza.

Speakers included Sarah Pickles from Right to Protest WA, primary school student Sakeenah Azizi, Palestinian-Australian Dareen Allagta, Sam Wainwright from the WA Anti-War Collective and Neda Blackwood from Teachers for Palestine WA.

The crowd were moved to tears by a performance from musical duo the Paddystinians — Johny Bravo and Ozzie Hishmeh.

A Paddle out for Palestine was held in Muloobinba/Newcastle on November 14, as part of Rising Tide’s Paddle for the Planet at Horseshoe Beach. Rachel Evans from City of Sydney for Palestine reminded the crowd that war and occupation is a climate issue.

NSW Greens MLC Sue Higginson said climate and Palestine protests are both being targeted by the Minns government’s undemocratic anti-protest laws. She said Newcastle City Council’s ban on Rising Tide events on council land would also apply to Palestine solidarity rallies.

title: Calvary takeover raises questions over hospital licences and access to VAD
content:
The proposed takeover of 14 former Healthscope hospitals by Catholic healthcare provider Calvary Health Care is facing scrutiny over competition, corporate accountability and the future availability of lawful healthcare services, including voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Calvary’s proposed acquisition includes six NSW hospitals: Newcastle Private, Hunter Valley Private, Norwest, Lady Davidson, The Hills Private and The Sydney Clinic.

Calvary has confirmed it will not offer or facilitate VAD in any acquired hospital. Other excluded services under its Catholic healthcare guidelines include in vitro fertilisation (IVF) and assisted reproductive technologies, elective terminations, vasectomies, tubal ligation and gender care procedures.

The implications are particularly significant in the Hunter. Newcastle Private has an established role in providing VAD services. Go Gentle Australia reports that the hospital is understood to receive approximately one or two VAD requests each week.

Calvary says patients requesting VAD will continue to receive compassionate care and that appropriate pathways will be explored. However, transferring seriously ill patients elsewhere can create considerable practical, clinical and personal difficulties, particularly near the end of life.

title: Union slams Qantas’ plan to outsource 850 jobs
