author: John Mullen
title: Update from France: Towards an explosive general strike?
content:
The sharp upturn in class struggle continues in France, with school students and workers demanding more for ordinary people and far less for bankers and billionaires.

The Emmanuel Macron government is setting up ever more authoritarian institutions and practices, demanding harsh sentences for those arrested, and mutilating teenagers, while making minor concessions. The trade union leaderships are calling, mostly half-heartedly, for mass strike action this week. An explosion is possible.

The hundreds of demonstrations on October 24 and 31 were a major victory for the movement. The government's attempt to scare people off the streets failed. Despite bans and curfews and a solemn presidential speech ("we recommend that people do not demonstrate"), despite invented figures about injured cops and the cost of damage to public buildings, the movement is going forward.

Many were too frightened to go to these protests (two more people were mutilated by cops on the 24th), but more turned up, in an atmosphere of joyous revolt. Support is flooding in from very varied places: the magistrates' union, for example, has denounced the "brutality" of police action, a group of Catholic activists published an open letter to their right-wing bishops entitled "We are proud to take part in the uprising", and the Louvre museum was blockaded last week by Fine Arts students.

The repression was ratcheted up. For the 31st, demonstrations were banned in many city centres and peripheral routes were imposed. More than 100 towns and cities have been affected by curfews or restrictions on assembly.

This week, using the excuse of the rioting in mid-October, Macron is trying to push through parliament a new law. It increases penalties for looting, but would also impose heavy punishment for refusing to leave a demonstration when the police tell you to; it would give police the power to ban individuals from attending protests for up to three years, and allow the authorities to confiscate wages or social benefits of people "present in an assembly" where looting takes place (even if the individuals involved are not accused of any offence).

The far right, which hopes to win the presidency next May, applauds every new repressive measure.

The government seems to make additional minor concessions each week. We have seen 3000 replacement teachers hired, smaller classes (of 28 pupils) announced for 15-year-olds, 15,000 more student places promised in higher education, small increases in grants for poorer students, and more loans for regional governments to rebuild crumbling high schools.

This week Macron announced "a complete remoulding" of the hated Parcoursup platform, which controls who gets into which university … in 2028, long after the next elections! Some concessions answer student demands directly, but far more is needed.

Working-class combativity has long protected some aspects of French education from neoliberalism: enrolling in university costs less than €300 a year, for example. But this movement is not a defensive one. It is demanding more: 250,000 more places in higher education and €5 billion for school buildings, for a start.

As high schools and universities finished their autumn break on November 2, there was little sign of calm. A regional university student coordinating meeting, with representatives from a dozen universities, met for the second time on October 31: just one example of the important grassroots initiatives building the revolt.

That same day, almost all docks in France were closed as workers struck both against war and against proposed cuts in welfare being discussed in parliament. Their demands include an increase in the minimum wage for all workers.

As I write, the general strike for November 5 is being prepared, in support of the high schools and for increases in wages and hirings. It will be huge.

After a delay by union leaderships — which it is difficult not to describe as criminal — one month after the beginning of the movement, mass strike action has finally been called across the economy by five of the six biggest union confederations.

One of the biggest, the General Confederation of Workers (CGT), is asking strikers to organise workplace meetings and to "generalise the strike on the 5th November and afterwards". (The "renewable strike", re-voted in general meetings every couple of days, is an excellent tradition in the French workers' movement, but it can also be used as an excuse by leaderships to avoid organising stronger action themselves.)

This mix — of a long young people’s revolt the government will not satisfy, rising anger among workers about the cost of living, and a budget being prepared by Macron ‘s government this month aiming at slashing tens of billions of euros from public spending — may be explosive.

In the public sector in France less than 20% of workers are members of a union, and in the private sector less than 10%. One reason for these low figures is that many benefits of union influence are available to non-members. Millions of non-members nevertheless vote for, and are represented by, union candidates for health and safety committees, company councils, industrial tribunals, regional and sectoral wages councils, and other such bodies. Agreements signed by trade unions generally apply to all workers.

The right to strike is part of the French constitution, and non-union workers are legally fairly well protected by the strike declarations made by unions. This relatively solid legal protection means it is very common, on days of action, to have minorities in a workplace taking strike action. One school or bus depot might have 20% on strike, another 80%.

A key historical weakness of the union movement here is its division into six — sometimes competing — confederations. In some sectors, workers tend to just join the biggest union in their workplace. Frequently, though, people choose the union according to their politics. The CGT (which used to be extremely close to the Communist Party) is generally more combative than the French Democratic Confederation of Labour (CFDT). Solidaires (Solidarity) is the most combative and the most left-wing, and less politicised workers don't generally join it.

The bosses and the government can play the federations off against each other, and the union leaders from the more combative confederations can and do use the excuse that "the others weren't ready to fight" to give up the struggle quickly themselves.

National union leaders in France do not receive the exorbitant salaries their counterparts in countries like Britain do, but they are still professional negotiators, and have a strong interest in movements not exploding out of their control.

During the movement to defend pensions in 2023, the big unions called at least 11 one-day strikes, generally a week or two apart. After each day of action, all six confederations met behind closed doors to decide what to do next, and always agreed to move at the pace of the slowest. The result was that the movement did not achieve its aims. There should have been mass rallies in front of the building during each of those meetings!

Rank-and-file workers may vote on the 5th to extend the strike, and this is the main hope for an escalation. But those who say the union leaders should be completely ignored are mistake. We pay their wages, they have mass influence, and we should demand loudly that they lead a general strike. There is easily enough support in the country to make this a realistic option. The government is rattled, so much so that this week they are talking about raising the national minimum wage (by a little). After the May 1968 revolt, with 10 million on strike, the minimum wage was raised by 35%, so the best strategy is not hard to work out.

The upcoming presidential election is on everyone's mind, especially as polling suggests a second-round showdown between fascist Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the radical-left France Insoumise (FI). Placards supporting Mélenchon are a common sight among protesters; FI MPs are actively backing the movement and opposing police violence, drawing loud applause at demonstrations. Meanwhile, right-wing presidential hopeful Bruno Retailleau has gone so far as to call for the organisation to be banned.

What happens over the next couple of weeks will heavily shape the broader political landscape and the elections ahead. Escalation is needed now.

[John Mullen is a revolutionary socialist living in the Paris region, and a supporter of the France Insoumise. His website is randombolshevik.org.]

author: John Tully
title: Australia can build public housing, end homelessness
content:
I often walk my dog in Nipaluna/Hobart’s beautiful Rivulet Linear Park, which winds up from the city to the foothills of Mount Wellington. If you’re lucky, you can spot a platypus in the rivulet, there are flocks of gorgeously plumed parrots, and the marsupial population is thriving.

But that’s not all you’ll see, for half-hidden in the bushes there are tent encampments: places of last resort for some of Lutruwita/Tasmania’s homeless people. Others huddle on pieces of cardboard in shop doorways in the CBD or in other parks.

Sleeping rough exposes people to the vagaries of the elements, the threat of theft and violence and a constant battle to maintain good health and sanitation.

A fine line now separates countless numbers of working-class people from a similar fate. With the country’s median rents at $705 per week — an increase of 40.6% in the past five years — half of all people who live in rental accommodation are struggling to put food on the table and pay rent and other bills.

About 45% of families with children struggle to buy sufficient food — an estimated 3.6 million people, 69% of whom report they are facing food insecurity for the first time.

The link between the cost-of-living crisis and soaring rents is clear: 1.26 million households are forced to pay more than 30% of their disposable income on rent, which doesn’t leave much for food, utilities, education and medical care.

This crisis disproportionately impacts renters — though this is not to downplay the struggles of many to pay their mortgages with rising interest rates.

Unforeseen bills can send renters into a downward spiral of debt and homelessness. Elderly and middle-aged women, often with little savings to fall back on, can find themselves out on the street.

About 48% of 18–34-year-olds find themselves in precarious living circumstances.

While the United States/Israeli war on Iran turbocharged the cost-of-living crisis by forcing up the price of fuel and fertilisers, this conjunctural crisis only added to the existing pressures in a country where millions of people are priced out of home ownership and are reliant on the private rental market.

It doesn’t have to be this way. Australia is the third wealthiest country in terms of median wealth, and the fifth wealthiest in terms of average wealth.

However this wealth is not distributed evenly. The top 1% are wealthier than the bottom 50$ combined, and much of their wealth is in property and real estate.

With Labor, the Coalition and One Nation pushing politics further to the right, there is little challenge to the neoliberal dogmas that had led us to this crisis.

Those three parties are firmly wedded to the private rental market. Indeed, many politicians have a personal interest in maintaining it.

According to the Guardian, at least 55% of federal politicians own multiple properties, and between 50 to 92 are actively receiving rental income.

Meanwhile, public housing has declined to only 4% of housing stock.

This is an ideological choice with disastrous consequences. While Australia does better than the US, where less than 1% of households live in any form of social or public housing, we compare poorly with most OECD countries.

Countries like the Netherlands (29%), Austria (24%), Denmark (21%), Sweden (17%) and Britain (17%) have far greater percentages of public housing stock than Australia. In Vienna, and other city centres that have consciously prioritised public housing, that figure can rise to more than 50%.

Social housing is nothing new — at least to those who care to look.

I recently visited the oldest public housing project in the world, the Fuggerei, in the southern German city of Augsburg, founded in 1521. The project’s museum points out that “people have continuously been living in the Fuggerei for half a millennium”.

One of the early residents was Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s great-grandfather, the impoverished bricklayer, Franz Mozart. “When the project’s major donor, the banker Jakob Fugger, died in 1525, there were 52 houses in the complex. Today, the Fuggerei consists of 140 flats in 67 houses, with other buildings for administration, a museum and workshops.”

The Fuggerei is not a ghetto of poverty and despair. It is a beautiful place, with homes meeting modern living standards with heating, modern bathrooms, television and the internet.

It has some strict conditions for residence, designed for “Catholic Augsburg residents in need”, who must contribute three prayers a day and 88 euro cents in annual rent.

If such a project could be built and maintained for more than 500 years, why is it that a wealthy country like Australia fares so poorly?

Safe, secure, affordable and well-maintained housing should be regarded as a human right, not as a cash cow for wealthy landlords.

author: Chris Slee
title: Forum discusses solidarity with Russian political prisoners
content:
A film screening was held in Naarm/Melbourne on November 1 to highlight the plight of Russian political prisoners and their families. The film features statements from the families of Russian political prisoners.

It was part of the Freedom Zone festival, organised to raise awareness and support for Russian political prisoners. This was the first event the organisation has held in Australia.

The film was introduced by Petr Kuzmin, who was born in Russia and now lives in Naarm. He told the audience that repression has intensified since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. He said people can be imprisoned for up to 15 years for criticising the war.

Freedom Zone said that people in Russia are “going to prison for a social media post, a donation, a hand-written sign, or for saying out loud they are against the war”.

It said at least 1680 people are being held as political prisoners, and more than 5500 people had been detained on politically motivated and unlawful grounds.

After the film, a video discussion was held with several family members of prisoners. One of those who featured in the film and joined the discussion was Kseniia Kagarlitskaya, daughter of well-known socialist writer and activist Boris Kagarlitsky, who was imprisoned for his anti-war views.

title: Forum discusses corruption and inhumanity in offshore detention regime
content:
The Refugee Action Collective Victoria (RAC) held a public forum in Naarm/Melbourne on October 26 to discuss the Anthony Albanese government’s policy of sending refugees to detention centres on remote islands.

Despite Albanese’s promise to end the offshore detention regime, about 100 refugees are currently held on Naoero (formerly Nauru). Previously refugees had been sent to Manus Island in Papua New Guinea (PNG), before its Supreme Court ruled this illegal.

Keynote speaker Nik Feik, an investigative journalist who has uncovered details about the offshore detention regime, said the system was corrupt. He said contractors receive hundreds of millions of dollars to run these centres, yet the refugees do not receive sufficient food and other supplies. “Where does the money go?”, he asked.

Feik said aircraft safety problems, audit reports and money handling processes had been ignored.

He raised concerns about Nauru Airlines, which owns seven Boeing 737 planes paid for by Australia. Naoero has a population of 12,000 and receives only 200 visitors each year. He said the planes had been used to take the families of political leaders on holidays.

Australia is committed to paying Naeoro $2.3 billion over 20 years in return for holding refugees and others deported from Australia.

author: Kavita Naidu
title: Kavita Naidu: You cannot destroy the Global South for the Global North’s renewable transition
content:
Kavita Naidu is an international human rights lawyer and feminist climate activist from Fiji. She delivered this speech at the No Cop-Outs at COP31: Climate Action Now rally at Sydney Town Hall on Gadigal Country, on October 24.

For the Pacific, going above 1.5 degrees is a death sentence we will not be quiet about.

The 1.5 degree threshold is not only anchored in the International Court of Justice (ICJ), it was also what the Pacific pushed for in the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.

For the first time we have a very powerful legal floor, and you can see in Australia there are legal cases which will establish what these advisory opinions mean in practice.

Pacific rejects false climate solutions

Pacific community service organisations met in Tuvalu ahead of Pre-COP in Fiji to issue the Funafuti Call for Climate Justice, which speaks for Pacific peoples. The rallying cry was “Lose Tuvalu, Lose our World”.

The Pacific is calling for an immediate phase out of coal, oil and gas and an end to new exploration, licensing, expansion and subsidies, with developed states phasing out first and fastest.

We are rejecting all false solutions, including carbon capture and storage, nuclear energy, offsetting, geoengineering and “managed transition pathways” as substitutes for cutting production.

We reject deep-sea mining, we reject a “just transition” based on green and blue colonialism, opening frontiers of dispossession of land and oceans to sate the need for developed states to transition.

A transition for who? And a transition for what? We are not questioning the consumption of energy as a problem, we are simply looking at the source of energy and we need to beyond this.

You cannot destroy and extract from the Global South to suit the transition needs of the Global North, that is not just and equitable.

We do not understand, because so much of it is greenwashed, but the rush for critical rare earth minerals is not just for solar panels, it is tied to the militarisation of this region. It is tied to missiles and drones.

You just need to see the billions the Australian government is putting into militarisation, because they want to go for our land and oceans and they need a military to protect those resources.

The Funafati Call rejects a securitised, militarised and nuclearised Pacific. It names AUKUS, the Papua New Guinea–Australia Mutual Defence Treaty (Pukpuk Treaty) and the Vuvale Union as attempts to seize control of our economic resources and make us beholden to what the Australian government demands of us.

We condemn all missile testing in our waters and we condemn any future weapons testing in our waters.

We assert our right to remain on our islands with dignity. We reject mobility deals traded against the sovereignty and security of our people.

The Pacific is a region that is still occupied. Struggles for self-determination continue in West Papua, Guam, Kanaky and Tahiti.

We cannot talk about climate justice without recognising self-determination of the indigenous people who continue to be on the frontlines of the worst climate impacts in this region.

This is why we must call out our Pacific leaders for endorsing Zionism by supporting Israel at the United Nations, opening Israeli embassies in the region and signing “development cooperation” deals.

We reject endorsing a genocidal state and commit to tackling the scourge of Zionist fundamentalism on our islands.

The other thing about the Pacific that people don’t understand is that we have among the highest rates of violence against women in the world. We recognise that we must incorporate gender justice into our climate justice campaigns.

That includes recognising and redistributing unpaid care, social protection guarantees and attention to gender-based violence and sexual and reproductive health rights.

The Pacific has also been very progressive in recognising how artificial intelligence and data centres are coming for us. We already have data centres being built, subsea cables and other digital infrastructure in the region, but their energy, water and emissions footprints are not being disclosed.

The Pacific asserts data sovereignty and the protection of indigenous knowledge from AI. We also question the duality of purpose of AI and its use for military surveillance and intelligence.

We will not be complicit in killing people in other parts of the world by providing the infrastructure in our region.

According to the ICJ ruling, a state that fails to protect the climate may be committing an internationally wrongful act. A state in breach must stop, guarantee it will not repeat the conduct, and make full reparation.

We charge Australia with breaking not just its word, but its law and its neighbours’ trust. It tells the Pacific it is “family”, but hypocritically keeps on approving new fossil fuel projects that drown our home.

Australia’s climate policy is a fossil fuel export policy with a climate strategy stapled to the front. It offers climate solutions with one hand, while driving the crisis with the other.

Australia has spent $62.6 billion on military this year, and has promised to lift military spending to 3% of gross domestic product by 2033. AUKUS will cost more than $400 billion over 30 years.

And the war machine is burning the planet. The Department of Defence produces the majority of public sector emissions, but has refused to publish detailed emissions data since 2012. That reporting never includes the emissions generated through military supply chains.

This is not an oversight. Governments go on about net zero but don’t count their military emissions.

The Australian government keeps paying polluters rather than giving climate reparations it owes to the Pacific and others for the harm that it has caused. It spent $16.3 billion on fossil fuel subsidies in 2025–26, while claiming there is no money for care, for disability, for loss and damage.

In October last year, Australia and the United States signed a critical minerals framework to secure supply chains for defence and advanced technology. It backed in $8.5 billion worth of projects including a gallium refinery in WA.

Australian companies’ complicity

We charge the Australia government, public pension funds and extractive industries with committing violence across the Global South.

Research by an international consortium of investigative journalists identified more than 150 publicly-traded Australian mining companies holding roughly 1500 licenses across 33 African nations.

These firms have been implicated in hundreds of worker and community deaths, environment pollution, displacement and labour abuses.

OK Tedi poisoned a river system in Papua New Guinea; BHP was behind the Mariana Dam collapse in Brazil; the Panguina mine, owned by Rio Tinto, left Bougainville with a toxic legacy and the company spent five decades refusing to own it; Rio Tinto mines have poisoned drinking water in Anosy region, one of Madagascar’s poorest; 70 people were massacred at Kilwa in the Democratic Republic of Congo by a Perth-based company called Anvil, which used its employees to transport soldiers, with no accountability in Australia; and the list continues.

Australian companies get away with behaviour offshore that they would never get away with here. They do it to my home and across the Global South. The harm always falls on Indigenous peoples, on women carrying the work of survival and recovery and on island nations.

This is a deliberate design of a settler-colony obsessed with protecting capitalism.

The Pacific named climate change the single greatest threat to their security. Canberra heard them and bought nuclear submarines.

Militarism and extractivism are not two separate stories. One digs the resources. The other guards it. Both treat the Pacific as territory to be secured rather than as peoples to be protected.

When the Pacific asks for loss and damage finance, it is told the coffers are bare. There is always another billion for the war machine. We are not asking for ambition. We are demanding cessation. No new coal and gas. No licenses. No approvals. End the subsidies. Pay what is owed.

We need to follow what Gen Z is doing all over the world, we need to mobilise at scale, disrupt and get angry. And we need it now.

title: Crisafulli accused of silencing criticism of ‘cruel’ youth crime laws
content:
Queensland’s Liberal National Party (LNP) government has been accused of cutting funding to non-government organisations for criticising its push to criminalise youth offenders.

The Youth Advocacy Centre, a vocal critic of the government’s Adult Crime, Adult Time (ACAT) laws, said the LNP had stripped $3 million in funding as a punishment for speaking out.

Several frontline organisations have accused the LNP of trying to intimidate them into silence and failing to include them in review processes.

The allegations were made as the David Crisafulli government passed its Breach Bail, Go To Jail laws which, alongside ACAT, increase the penalties for youth offending and reduce opportunities for non-carceral sentencing.

These changes mean children who would have once been sentenced to community-based supervision may be incarcerated for the same offence. They will be subject to sentencing guidelines previously reserved for adult offenders.

Young people who breach bail conditions for certain offences will be subject to a mandatory minimum sentence of one year in detention.

Evidence suggests this will increase youth re-offending as young people are further exposed to the criminal justice system. These laws will increase exposure to Queensland’s overcrowded and inhumane youth detention and watchhouse facilities.

title: States refuse to act on South East Asia’s transboundary haze
content:
The recent State of Global Air report published by the Health Effects Institute and published on the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service website, identified Southeast Asia, East Asia, and Oceania as the region with the fourth-highest death rates attributable to air pollution, at 100 deaths per 100,000 people.

The World Health Organization reports that “when inhaled, health-damaging pollutants including small particulates can penetrate deep into the respiratory system and enter the bloodstream, allowing them to reach almost all organs within the body, including but not limited to cardiovascular, reproductive and metabolic systems, brain, liver and kidneys.”

The wildfires in parts of Indonesia, which started in early September, have impacted communities across South East Asia. Malaysian climate activists Syafiq Fadli and Huei Ting Cheong look at the origins of this toxic air pollution and why governments still refuse to take serious action to protect lives.

Transboundary haze has been a recurring environmental issue in Malaysia and the Southeast Asia region since the late 1990s, caused by slash-and-burn land clearing methods to cultivate palm oil plantations and a highly humid tropical climate with temperature fluctuations. It is a form of air pollution characterised by fine particles in the atmosphere that comprise pollutants such as smoke, dust, and industrial emissions

author: José Soeiro, Maria Manuel Rola
title: A new cycle of struggle in Portugal
content:
At the end of last June, the left and the labour movement in Portugal secured an unlikely victory: the government’s proposed labour reform, which would have overhauled the Labour Code from top to bottom, was defeated in parliament.

Public pressure was so intense — with two general strikes, dozens of protests and a campaign that rallied the majority of public opinion against the government’s violently regressive agenda — that the far right, fearful of the electoral consequences of seeing its support for such a thoroughly unpopular proposal through to the end, changed its position and ultimately joined forces with the left to vote down the government’s labour reform package.

This struggle ushered in a new cycle of confidence for the popular movement.

The government, which holds a minority in parliament, put labour issues on hold and sought to change the subject. It ensured that the Socialist Party [PS] abstained on the draft state budget, on the one hand, and, on the other, reached an agreement with the far right on a new rental law which, in practice, virtually eliminates any rights for tenants.

A two-month delay in paying rent can lead to eviction. There is no longer a cap on deposits for renting a property. The number of months’ rent a tenant must pay in advance when signing a tenancy agreement has been increased to three. The 2% cap on rent increases has been removed.

title: UN General Assembly votes to end US blockade of Cuba — again
content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-thirty countries voted in favour of the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba” on October 28, with 17 against and 25 abstentions.

Every year since 1992, the UNGA has overwhelmingly voted to end the blockade. However, this year, there was a rise in votes against and abstentions, likely reflective of new far-right governments — for example, in Colombia, Chile and Honduras — coming to power since last year’s vote. The US has also ramped up its international efforts to isolate Cuba through sanctions and threats of sanctions against countries that trade with Cuba.

This year’s vote took place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

content:
Finally, the ill-fitting mask on the ugly face of government policy comes off. In the sunset of his administration, French President Emmanuel Macron is facing a boiling, indignant movement that began with the protests of disgruntled students and has burgeoned into something much more significant.

Teachers at the Antoine de Saint-Exupéry High School in the southeastern Parisian suburb of Créteil went on strike over severe staff shortages, on September 17. content:
About 150 people filled the Ashfield Town Hall auditorium on October 10 for the Gadigal/Sydney premiere of environmental group Rising Tide’s new short film, Taking the Channel.

The film showcases the People’s Blockade of the world’s biggest coal port, which took place in Muloobinba/Newcastle, in November last year.

Taking the Channel features interviews with activists who took part in the blockade, as well as dramatic footage of the hundreds of people on their kayaks setting out from Horseshoe Beach to confront a giant coal ship attempting to pass through the Newcastle Port’s entrance.

During the film, it is revealed that several coal ships were directly turned around by the blockade, while up to a dozen others were cancelled by the authorities as a result of the mass action by activists.

Interviews with participants include a grandmother from Adelaide contemplating challenging the law by going out on the water: “Am I able to go through with it?” she says. title: Reject the AUKUS death machine, join the fight for the future
content:
The nuclear powered submarine USS Colorado docked at the HMAS Stirling naval base on Menadup/Garden Island, five kilometres from Rockingham in Perth’s southern suburbs, on October 27.

The vessel is in port for a month of maintenance exercises in preparation for the Submarine Rotational Force — West program which will start in September next year, being the first of four United States’ and one British nuclear powered submarines based at HMAS Stirling.

Its arrival was an opportunity for Labor to insist that AUKUS is “on track”, without resolving any of the significant cost and time blow-outs associated with the plan to build the SSN-AUKUS class submarines.

It also means that HMAS Stirling has become a de facto US navy base, with its submarines and crew not just visiting, but stationed in Western Australia, allowing the US to qualitatively step up its presence in the Indian Ocean.

content:

author: Cas Smith
title: Brazil: Lula’s election victory was won in the streets
content:
Australia’s Brazilian community joined their compatriots worldwide in a wave of street mobilisations in support of incumbent President Luiz Inácio “Lula” da Silva, ahead of his election victory on October 25.

Lula, who was first elected president in 2002, pulled ahead of right-wing opponent Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro — winning the second round run-off election by 4.4 million votes.

Significantly, this came after Bolsonaro won the first round on October 4, which prompted Brazilians to hit the streets in a significant movement to bolster Lula’s profile, and to prevent a “second Bolsonaro” presidency.

Students and the country’s working class largely led these mobilisations, which included a gathering of more than one million Lula supporters on Rio de Janeiro’s Copacabana Beach the day before the election.

title: Students, staff rally against proposed ‘mega university’ merger plan
content:
About 500 people, including students, academics and concerned members of the community, rallied at Western Australian Parliament in Boorloo/Perth on October 21 to oppose the shock proposal by the state Labor government to merge three major universities.

Organised by the National Union of Students (NUS) and student guilds of Curtin University, Murdoch University and the University of Western Australia (UWA), the rally came only a week after WA education minister Tony Buti unveiled details of the merger plan, which he said would allow the state’s tertiary education sector to remain “highly competitive, accessible and relevant”.

title: Accessible tram stop campaigners try to board Sydney Road tram
content:
After being ignored by the Victorian government for three-and-a-half years, the Sydney Road Accessible Tram Stops (SATS) campaign held an action on October 23.

A group of about 30 people, with and without mobility aids, attempted to board a tram on Sydney Road to highlight the inaccessibility.

While Sydney Road has many different classes of trams that run along it, campaigners waited for a low floor tram because it is those that would be accessible if tram stops were upgraded.

These could be used by people with mobility aids such as wheelchairs, walkers and crutches, but also by people with prams and shopping trolleys.

The rally waited for more than 20 minutes for a low floor tram to approach. Once it arrived, campaigners tried to board.

Protesters sang and chanted as they unsuccessfully attempted to board the tram.

One person had come with a ramp, and pointed out that the only way someone with a mobility issue could use a tram is to carry around a heavy ramp with them.

To highlight how long the campaign has been going — as well as previous public transport and disability rights campaigns — a model skeleton, named Briony, sat in a wheelchair, was the mascot for the day.

Organisers said “Briony” had been waiting so long for accessible tram stops to be built on Sydney Road that she died in her wheelchair.

title: International convoy seeks to boost solidarity with Ukraine from the bottom up
content:
Alfons Bech is the International Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (INSU) trade union coordinator and a member of the Coordination Group of the International Solidarity Convoy to Ukraine, organising its southern route from Barcelona to Kyiv.

Green Left’s Dick Nichols spoke to Bech about the convoy’s goals and organisation.

Where did the idea of the convoy come from?

It emerged on the second anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion [February 22, 2024], when the European Network for Solidarity with Ukraine (ENSU, now INSU) proposed organising a large international delegation of trade unionists to an event in Kyiv that the Federation of Trade Unions of Ukraine (FPU) and the Confederation of Free Trade Unions of Ukraine prepared with the support of the European Trade Union Confederation.

Trade unions participated in very large numbers, but online. Only one delegation went to Kyiv, representing the Catalan affiliate of the all-Spanish General Union of Workers (UGT).

The UGT delegation was very shocked by what they saw, but very pleased to have been there in person. They saw the devastation Russia had caused in Bucha and in the neighbourhoods of Kyiv, took part in the distribution of some material aid and got to know a little about Ukrainian culture.

title: Students demand climate action and ‘No Cop-Outs at COP31’
content:

Students gathered at Sydney Town Hall to hear musicians performing climate-related songs and from speakers, before marching to the NSW Labor Party headquarters.

Performances by the Sydney Knitting Nannas, Eva Diana and Gailla set an optimistic and energetic tone.

title: Allega Spender pushes to remove religious exemptions against LGBTIQ students, teachers
content:
The Sex Discrimination and Fair Work Amendment (Equality in Treatment in Religious Schools) Bill 2026, introduced on October 12, seeks to repeal the offending exemptions in federal sex discrimination law as well as removing the related provisions in federal workplace relations law. It also extends protections to associates of those who are captured under the current exemptions.

Section 38 of the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (SDA) makes it lawful for religious education institutions to discriminate against a teacher, student or contract worker due to their “sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, marital or relationship status or pregnancy”.

author: Ben Radford
title: US must end its cruel blockade of Cuba
content:
Every year since 1992, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) has overwhelmingly voted to end the United States government’s cruel and illegal economic blockade of Cuba. One-hundred-and-sixty-five countries voted last year for the resolution on the “Necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”, with just six against.

This year’s vote, on October 28, takes place as escalating US economic warfare against Cuba is causing a devastating humanitarian crisis. The blockade’s impacts have been characterised as a “silent genocide”, severely restricting Cubans’ access to food, medicine, equipment and fuel, and impacting every aspect of daily life.

The Cuban government submitted its annual report to the UNGA in September, detailing last year’s impacts of the US blockade. Between March last year and February this year, the blockade inflicted more than US$8 billion worth of damages.

The economic cost of just four days of the blockade amounts to the cost of all fuel imports needed to meet Cuba’s demand.

title: NSW Labor to introduce law overriding High Court coal mine ruling
content:
The NSW Labor government will introduce a law to allow MACH Energy to expand output at its contested Mount Pleasant coal mine in the Upper Hunter region of NSW, in response to a High Court ruling that invalidated the expansion approval.

The High Court ruled on October 7 that the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider how pollution from its coal would affect the region. It also emphasised that the IPC must consider Scope 3 — downstream emissions from coal burned elsewhere, including overseas — as part of its approval process.

Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) first challenged the IPC’s approval in 2023 in the NSW Land and Environment Court. Following a protracted legal battle, DAMSHEG had its case upheld in the High Court.

Premier Chris Minns told the ABC on October 19 that he was moving to protect jobs that would be “on the line”. He said the new law would “guarantee” 400 direct jobs until 2032 — the deadline for the temporary extension MACH Energy sought and was given, even though the High Court was considering MACH Energy’s case against DAMSHEG.

The mining corporation wants a licence to mine thermal coal until 2048 — something Minns and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese support.

title: Hunter Jobs Alliance says new law on coal transition gives hope
content:

content:

While many of those old superstitions have worn thin, they have been replaced by the myth that the mega rich are where they are because they have brilliant minds, or have worked their way to the top.

But this myth is also wearing thinner — thanks to United States President Donald Trump’s narcissistic outbursts and the obscene growth in the wealth of the mega rich.

title: The climate-changing policy behind Türkiye’s floods
content:

The same storms flooded five other provinces, including Antalya, which will be host to COP31 in less than four weeks.

Istanbul alone recorded 1277 floods and 15 landslides; schools closed the next day.

None of this was a surprise. The day before the state meteorological service forecast about 21–50 millimetres of rain for Istanbul; parts of the city’s north received nearly 194mm. Cities are meant to be built for the worst case scenario, not the forecast.

title: City of Sydney for Palestine joins calls for council to boycott Airbnb
content:

Airbnb is a target of the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement because of its role in enabling tourism in illegal Israeli settlements in the Occupied West Bank.

Airbnb helps normalise Israel’s occupation, apartheid and dispossession of Palestinians from their homeland by listing and profiting from accommodation on stolen Palestinian land.

Airbnb is helping turn occupied land into a tourism market. It is helping normalise dispossession. It is making money while Palestinians are denied freedom, safety and return.

Airbnb is also part of the housing crisis in Australia.

There is severe housing stress in the Sydney, where Rents are rising and vacancies are low. Meanwhile, thousands of homes are being used as short-term rentals through platforms like Airbnb.

Airbnb and short-term rental platforms allow homes to be converted into commercial tourist accommodation, while renters are pushed further into crisis.
